stem: A 35-year-old woman with a history of acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is admitted for chemotherapy, which includes the drugs fludarabine and cytarabine. She is to receive irradiated blood. What is the reason for receiving irradiated blood in this situation?
options: To prevent toxicity from bacterial endotoxin
To prevent transfusion-associated graft versus host disease
To prevent transfusion-related acute lung injury
explanation:
To prevent transfusion-associated graft versus host disease
The reason for receiving irradiated blood in this situation is to prevent transfusion-associated graft versus host disease (TA-GVHD). Patients who receive the purine analogue fludarabine will have low numbers of T-cells. If the blood is not irradiated, white cells that are left in the transfused blood can cause a condition called transfusion-associated graft versus host disease. This canbe effectively prevented by irradiating the blood that will be transfused.

To prevent CMV infection
To prevent CMV infection is incorrect. Irradiation does not prevent CMV infection.

To prevent mast cell degranulation
To prevent mast cell degranulation is incorrect. The reason for receiving irradiated blood in this situation is not to prevent mast cell degranulation but to prevent transfusion-associated graft versus host disease.

To prevent toxicity from bacterial endotoxin
To prevent toxicity from bacterial endotoxin is incorrect. Irradiating a blood transfusion will not prevent bacterial contamination.

To prevent transfusion-related acute lung injury
To prevent transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) is incorrect. Irradiating blood will not prevent TRALI. Irradiating the blood transfusion will destroy the donor T-lymphocytes in the blood that are responsible for the development of transfusion-associated graft versus host disease.

stem: Which one of the following statements regarding iron deficiency anaemia is MOST accurate?
options: It is most commonly caused by dietary deficiency
Pins and needles in the hands and feet may indicate early peripheral neuropathy
Splenomegaly occurs in up to 50% of cases
Koilonychia is characteristic and rarely seen in other forms of anaemia
explanation:
Koilonychia is characteristic and rarely seen in other forms of anaemia
Spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia) are characteristic and are rarely described in other forms of anaemia.

It is most commonly caused by dietary deficiency
It is most commonly caused by dietary deficiency is incorrect. Although dietary deficiency can play a role in iron deficiency, excessive blood loss, either as a result of gastrointestinal or menstrual blood loss, is more common.

Pins and needles in the hands and feet may indicate early peripheral neuropathy
Pins and needles in the hands and feet is incorrect. This is not the most accurate statement regarding iron deficiency and such symptoms not very common at all.

Splenomegaly occurs in up to 50% of cases
Splenomegaly is incorrect. This should not be associated with iron deficiency.

Reticulocyte count is often elevated.

stem: Which antibody is most associated with her prolonged APTT?
explanation:
Anti-phospholipid antibody
Anti-phospholipid antibodies are likely to be found in the serum of this 35-year-old woman. She has typical features of the anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome, and actually has had recurrent miscarriages and livedo reticularis. She has a prolonged APTT. Despite the prolonged APTT, such patients are at risk of paradoxical venous thrombotic events.

Anti-centromere antibody
Anti-centromere antibody is incorrect. Anti-centromere antibodies are associated with systemic sclerosis.

Anti-D antibody
Anti-D antibody is incorrect. Anti-D antibodies lead to haemolytic disease of the new-born.

Anti-nuclear antibody
Anti-nuclear antibody is incorrect. Anti-nuclear antibodies are associated with SLE.

Anti-smooth muscle antibody.

stem: Which of the following investigations is most likely to be positive with respect to confirming primary polycythaemia?
explanation:
JAK-2 mutation analysis
This man has evidence of a raised haemoglobin and a thrombocytosis, suggesting an underlying primary polycythaemia. The JAK-2 mutation is present in greater than 95% of patients with primary polycythaemia and can be done on a peripheral blood sample.

Bone marrow biopsy
Bone marrow biopsy is incorrect. Bone marrow biopsy is usually unnecessary if patients have typical features of polycythaemia on the full blood count, and are positive for the JAK-2 mutation.

Platelet aggregation studies
Platelet aggregation studies is incorrect. Platelet aggregation studies is not a test used in polycythaemia investigation.

Serum urate
Serum urate is incorrect. Serum urate can be raised, reflecting increased cell turnover, but this is not helpful in defining the diagnosis of primary polycythaemia.

Vitamin B12 levels.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has been admitted with pulmonary embolism. After 7 days she develops an arterial thrombosis in her left leg. The platelet count is 40 × 10 9/l. Which drug is most likely to be responsible?
explanation:
Intravenous heparin for acute treatment
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is caused by IgG antibodies that recognise multimolecular complexes of platelet factor 4 and heparin. HIT occurs in as many as 5% of certain high-risk populations. Typically, the fall in platelet count begins 5–10 days after starting heparin. However, in any patient who has received heparin within the past 100 days, the platelet count can fall abruptly on resuming heparin therapy, probably because of residual circulating HIT antibodies. Most patients with HIT develop venous or arterial thrombosis: Deep vein thrombosis Pulmonary embolism Major limb artery thrombosis Stroke Myocardial infarction Bilateral adrenal haemorrhagic necrosis – leading to acute or chronic adrenal failure (much less common than the above, but has been described) The thrombocytopenia is typically moderate in severity (median platelet count nadir 60 × 10 9/l), and the platelet count falls to less than 20 × 10 9/l in only 10% of patients. In at least 10% of patients the platelet count never drops below 150 × 10 9/l.

Bisacodyl for her constipation
Bisacodyl for her constipation is incorrect. Bisacodyl is not associated with thrombocytopenia.

Temazepam for night-time sleep
Temazepam for night-time sleep is incorrect. Temazepam is not associated with thrombocytopenia.

Tramadol for pain control
Tramadol for pain control is incorrect. Tramadol is not associated with thrombocytopenia.

Warfarin for continuous outpatient treatment.

stem: A 53-year-old man with antiphospholipid syndrome had two deep venous thromboses in the past. Which one of the following is the most appropriate anticoagulation regimen?
explanation:
Warfarin lifelong
Lifelong warfarin is the most appropriate anticoagulation for this man. He has the antiphospholipid antibody syndrome and has had two venous thrombotic events. Regardless of this man’s underlying condition, having two deep vein thromboses would require lifelong anticoagulation.

Aspirin
Aspirin is incorrect. This is insufficient anticoagulation. Aspirin is particularly useful for the prevention of arterial thrombosis associated with atherosclerosis, but not particularly effectivein the prevention of venous thrombotic events.

Aspirin and warfarin
Aspirin and warfarin is incorrect. This combination will result in higher rates of gastrointestinal bleeding.

Long-term heparin
Long-term heparin is incorrect. Long-term heparin is costly and uncomfortable, and lifelong warfarin is preferred. ThrombophiliaWarfarin for 6 months
Warfarin for 6 months is incorrect. Warfarin for 6 months is insufficient. This man has had two venous thrombotic events, that would require lifelong anticoagulation.

stem: Which one of the following is the most like diagnosis?
explanation:
Idiopathic thrombocytopaenic purpura
This lady has a relatively normal haemoglobin and white cell count, but a significant thrombocytopaenia. She appears otherwise well. This would therefore be consistent with ITP.

Anticoagulant abuse
Anticoagulant abuse is incorrect. Anticoagulant abuse would prolong the INR but would have no impact on the platelet count, so this is false.

Haemophilia B
Haemophilia B is incorrect. Haemophilia B only occurs in male patients as it is X-linked. This would not affect the platelet count and would prolong the APTT.

Thrombotic thrombocytopaenic purpura
Thrombotic thrombocytopaenic purpura (TTP) is incorrect. There are no clinical features such as cerebral or renal involvement to suggest this diagnosis. This is a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, and, in this patient, there is no anaemia. Patients with TTP are usually very unwell, which is not the clinical scenario presented here.

von Willebrand’s disease
von.

stem: You are asked to audit the use of low molecular weight versus unfractionated heparin in the hospital and provide commentary on the rationale for choosing between the two agents. Which of the following is true of the profile of low molecular weight heparin, (LMWH)?
options: Absorption is less for LMW heparin than for unfractionated heparin
It has a shorter half life
It has a lower incidence of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, (HIT)
Risk of bleeding is higher with LMW heparin
explanation:
It has a lower incidence of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, (HIT)
LMW heparin has a lower affinity for platelet factor 4 and therefore a lower incidence of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

Absorption is less for LMW heparin than for unfractionated heparin
Absorption is less for LMW heparin than for unfractionated heparin is incorrect. Bioavailability is higher for LMW heparin than for unfractionated heparin.

It has a shorter half life
It has a shorter half life is incorrect. The half-life of subcutaneous LMW heparin (3–6 h) is 2–4 times that of unfractionated heparin.

Risk of bleeding is higher with LMW heparin
Risk of bleeding is higher with LMW heparin is incorrect. There are only a small number of comparative studies, but evidence suggests the risk of bleeding is potentially less for LMW heparin vs unfractionated heparin.

Only unfractionated heparin activates antithrombin
Only unfractionated heparin activates antithrombin is incorrect. Both forms of heparin (ie unfractionated and low-molecular-weight (LMW) heparin) bind and activate antithrombin, accelerating the interaction of antithrombin with activated factor X (factor Xa) by 1000-fold.

stem: A 30-year-old pregnant female, who has reached 20 weeks, has a family history of a cousin with deep vein thromboses (DVTs). Her thrombophilia screen shows she is heterozygous for factor V Leiden. Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Seek medical attention for anticoagulation if the calf swells or she suffers pleuritic chest pain
explanation:
Seek medical attention for anticoagulation if the calf swells or she suffers pleuritic chest pain
The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists has guidelines on the prevention of venous thrombotic events in pregnancy. This lady essentially has two risk factors for venous thrombotic events during pregnancy, namely her family history and the fact that her thrombophilia screen shows that she is heterozygous for factor V Leiden. However, the details of the family history of deep vein thrombosis is important. This is only really important if it has occurred in a first degree family member (mother, father, brother, sister). One could consider anticoagulation either before or after the birth if there were additional risk factors present.

Aspirin 75 mg once daily
Aspirin 75 mg once daily is incorrect. This is not very effective in preventing venous thromboticevents, and if the decision was made to give prophylactic anticoagulation either before or after the birth, low-molecular-weight heparin is preferred.

Prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin
Prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin is incorrect. In the information that has been given thus far, there are not sufficient risk factors to warrant this at present. However, additional risk factors such as obesity, age greater than 35, being a current smoker or multiple pregnancies may influence this decision.

Prophylactic unfractionated heparin
Prophylactic unfractionated heparin is incorrect. If one did wish to give prophylactic anticoagulation, the lowmolecular-weight formulation of heparin is much more preferred.

Prophylactic warfarin
Prophylactic warfarin is incorrect. Prophylactic warfarin is contra-indicated in pregnancy owing to the risk of fetal abnormalities.

stem: A 32-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with symptoms of fatigue, cyanosis and shortness of breath. He has a history of recent exposure to nitrates through his occupation as a fertiliser factory worker. His physical examination reveals central cyanosis, but his oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Partial pressure of oxygen measurement by arterial blood gas
explanation:
Co-oximetry
Co-oximetry is the best test for diagnosing methaemoglobinaemia because it can directly measure methaemoglobin levels in the blood. Methaemoglobinaemia occurs when the iron in haemoglobin is oxidised from ferrous (Fe2 +) to ferric (Fe3 +), impairing its ability to bind and release oxygen efficiently. This condition results in functional anaemia and cyanosis despite normal partial pressure of oxygen and pulse oximetry readings, as seen in this patient’s presentation. Co-oximetry differentiates between various haemoglobin species, providing a precise measurement necessary for an accurate diagnosis.

Partial pressure of oxygen measurement by arterial blood gas
While arterial blood gas (ABG) measurement of partial pressure of oxygen may show normal or slightly reduced values in patients with methaemoglobinaemia due to intact alveolar-capillary diffusion gradients, this value does not provide definitive evidence needed for diagnosis. Some arterial blood gas analysers can measure Methemoglobin levels in the blood, which, along with other investigations such as co-oximetry, would be useful in the confirmation of a diagnosis of methaemoglobinaemia.

Full blood count
A full blood count (FBC) provides information about red cell indices such as haemoglobin concentration, haematocrit level and white cell counts but does not assess abnormal forms of haemoglobin like methaemoglobin. While FBC might reveal anaemia if present concurrently with other conditions affecting erythropoiesis or red cell survival, it cannot diagnose functional abnormalities caused by altered haemoglobin forms.

Pulse oximetry
Pulse oximetry measures peripheral arterial oxygen saturation based on light absorption by oxyhaemoglobin versus deoxyhaemoglobin. However, it cannot distinguish methaemoglobinaemia from other causes because both oxidised states absorb light similarly at wavelengths used by standard pulse oximeters. In cases like this, where patients present with cyanosis yet maintain high pulse oximeter readings above 90%, reliance solely on this method would be misleading without further co-oximetric verification.

Serum lactate level
Serum lactate levels indicate tissue hypoxia secondary to anaerobic metabolism but are non-specific indicators that could be elevated due to various causes, including sepsis or cardiogenic shock, rather than direct evidence pointing towards specific haematological disorders like methaemoglobinaemia itself, which requires targeted diagnostic tools such as co-oximetry rather than metabolic markers alone.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents 2 days postpartum with sudden onset left-sided chest pain and shortness of breath. She is tachycardic and has a respiratory rate of 24 breaths per minute. She is started on intravenous unfractionated heparin. She is started on warfarin the day after when a ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scan confirms a pulmonary embolus, but is slow to reach therapeutic anticoagulation and heparin is therefore continued. Eight days into the treatment she requires increasing doses of heparin to maintain a therapeutic activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT). On day ten she has a pale, pulseless and painful right foot. Which one of the following diagnostic laboratory results supports your clinical diagnosis?
options: A low protein C level of 43%
explanation:
A low platelet count of 50 ×109/l
This woman has received unfractionated heparin. By day ten, she has a pale, pulseless and painful right foot, which would be indicative of an arterial embolic event. This is despite heparin anticoagulation. Therefore, this is suspicious for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and a falling platelet count would be supportive of the clinical diagnosis.

A low factor VII assay
A low factor VII assay is incorrect. A low factor VII assay would pre-dispose to bleeding, and not a new arterial thrombotic event.

A low protein C level of 43%
A low protein C level of 43% is incorrect. A low protein C level of 43% has nothing to do with the suspected diagnosis of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. It should be noted, however, that protein C levels will fall with warfarin therapy, because protein C is a vitamin-K-dependent factor.

An APTT ratio of 1.7
An APTT ratio of 1.7 is incorrect. An APTT ratio of 1.7 would not be supportive of the clinical diagnosis of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

A prolonged international normalised ratio (INR)
Prolonged INR is incorrect. Prolonged INR would not be suggestive of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

stem: A 64-year-old lady presents with tiredness to her GP. Routine examination reveals 2 cm splenomegaly, and bloods reveal a WBC 15 × 10 9/l (neutrophils 90%), Hb 120 g/l, Plts 650 × 10 9/l. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Essential thrombocythaemia
This 64-year-old lady has a normal haemoglobin level. She has a neutrophilia, splenomegaly with a raised platelet count. This would therefore be compatible with essential thrombocythaemia. This is one of the myeloproliferative disorders. Mild splenomegaly is common, as is a neutrophil leucocytosis. Treatment in a lady of this age would be with a myelosuppressive agent such as hydroxycarbamide to reduce the platelet count, along with an anti-platelet drug such as aspirin.

ALL
ALL is incorrect. There is nothing to suggest an acute leukaemia here, such as the presence of blasts. In addition, patients with acute leukaemia would be expected to be cytopaenic, e.g. with a neutropaenia or thrombocytopaenia.

CLL
CLL is incorrect. There is no suggestion of a lymphocytosis here.

CML
CML is incorrect. In CML the white cell count is usually much, much higher, and it can be greater than 200 × 10 9/l.

Multiple myeloma.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents to the oncology clinic for review. He is currently managed with a multi-agent chemotherapy regime and complains of pains, predominantly in his feet, with loss of sensation. This is causing him difficulty in walking. On examination he has a peripheral sensory neuropathy affecting both feet, and loss of the Achilles tendon reflex bilaterally. Which of the following agents is most likely to have been responsible?
explanation:
Vincristine
Neuropathic pain, sensory loss, paraesthesiae, difficulty in walking, slapping gait, loss of deep tendon reflexes, ataxia, paresis, foot drop and cranial nerve palsies, especially ocular palsies and laryngeal nerve paralysis, are described in association with vincristine treatment. Frequently, there appears to be a sequence in the development of neuromuscular side effects. Initially, one may encounter only sensory impairment and paraesthesiae, with other symptoms appearing later. Other cytotoxic agents which commonly cause peripheral neuropathies are platinum agents (e.g. cisplatin, carboplatin) and taxanes (eg paclitaxel, docetaxel).

Cyclophosphamide
Cyclophosphamide is incorrect. Cyclophosphamide is known to result in haemorrhagic cystitis.

Doxorubicin
Doxorubicin is incorrect. Doxorubicin is associated with cardiac toxicity including heart failure and dilated cardiomyopathy.

Methotrexate
Methotrexate is incorrect. Methotrexate is associated with hepatic and pulmonary fibrosis.

Prednisolone
Prednisolone is incorrect. Prednisolone is associated with the development of the Cushingoid symptoms including weight gain, moon facies, skin thinning, stria, bruising, hypertension and impaired glucose tolerance.

stem: A 41-year-old man presents with a neck lump, weight loss and night sweats. On examination, you note he has hepatomegaly. Which one of the following is the likeliest diagnosis?
explanation:
High-grade B-cell non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma
High-grade B-cell non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma is the commonest type of high-grade lymphoma. It can be associated with B-symptoms such as weight loss and night sweats.

High-grade T-cell non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma
High-grade T-cell non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma is incorrect. T-cell lymphomas are very rare, with high-grade Bcell non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma being much more common.

Hodgkin’s disease
Hodgkin’s disease is incorrect. We are told that he has a neck lump, as well as hepatomegaly,so this would indicate disease above and below the diaphragm, ie at least stage III disease.This is unusual in Hodgkin’s disease.

Large-cell lung carcinoma
Large-cell lung carcinoma is incorrect. There is nothing in the history to particularly suggest thisas a diagnosis, such as a prolonged smoking history. Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma

Low-grade non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma
Low-grade non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma is incorrect. Low-grade non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma would be less likely to cause these symptoms.

stem: Which one of the following is the most likely explanation for the full blood count results seen here?
explanation:
Folic acid deficiency
This man has a macrocytic anaemia with a slightly low white cell count. Anti-endomysial antibodies are positive, indicating coeliac disease. He also has symptoms of malabsorption, namely diarrhoea and weight loss. The renal impairment is because of fluid loss and subsequent dehydration.

Alcoholic liver disease
Alcoholic liver disease is incorrect. The liver function tests are not even mentioned in this question and there is nothing in the question to suggest excessive alcohol intake.

Aplastic anaemia
Aplastic anaemia is incorrect. Aplastic anaemia would usually cause a pancytopenia with a very significant reduction in the platelet count.

Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism is incorrect. We are given no indication of thyroid results here and hypothyroidism would not be associated with coeliac disease.

Vitamin C deficiency
Vitamin C deficiency is incorrect. Vitamin C deficiency would not cause such a significant macrocytic anaemia and be associated with coeliac disease.

stem: A 28-year-old patient is undergoing a dental extraction. He has mild haemophilia A with factor VIII activity of around 5%. He has been given desmopressin prophylaxis. What is the mode of action of desmopressin?
options: Release stored von Willebrand factor and factor VIII
explanation:
Release stored von Willebrand factor and factor VIII
Both stored VWF and factor VIII are released in response to desmopressin. This increases availability and stability of factor VIII.

Antithrombin III action
Antithrombin III action is incorrect. The correct mode of action of desmopressin is to cause release of von Willebrand factor from the endothelium.

Increase in factor 10a
Increase in factor 10a is incorrect. The correct mode of action of desmopressin is to cause release of stored von Willebrand factor from the endothelium.

Prevention of fibrinolysis
Prevention of fibrinolysis is incorrect. The correct mode of action of desmopressin is to cause release of stored von Willebrand factor from the endothelium. Tranexamic acid could be given to this man in addition, which would act to inhibit fibrinolysis.

Increase production of factor VIII
Increase production of factor VIII is incorrect. The correct mode of action of desmopressin is to cause release of stored von Willebrand factor and factor VIII rather than increase production.

stem: You are reviewing a 35-year-old patient who presented to the Emergency Department with bleeding. His blood picture in the Emergency Department suggested disseminated intravascular coagulation, and unfortunately acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APML) was confirmed soon after his admission. He begins treatment with alltrans-retinoic acid (ATRA). Which one of the following descriptions best fits with the features of ATRA therapy?
options: APML carries a worse prognosis where remission is achieved compared with other types of AML
ATRA is usually given as maintenance therapy for 6 months after post-remission therapy is
ATRA promotes the differentiation of APML cells into mature granulocytes and apoptosis of these
ATRA should only be used during the acute period of DIC
explanation:
ATRA promotes the differentiation of APML cells into mature granulocytes and apoptosis of these
ATRA promotes the differentiation of APML cells into mature granulocytes and apoptosis of these cells The answer is ATRA promotes the differentiation of APML cells into mature granulocytes and apoptosis of these cells. ATRA does promote the differentiation of APML cells into mature granulocytes.This is its mechanism of action.

APML carries a worse prognosis where remission is achieved compared with other types of AML
APML carries a worse prognosis where remission is achieved compared with other types of AML is incorrect. APML is an eminently treatable and curable form of leukaemia, especially when the risk of life-threatening haemorrhage has been overcome.

ATRA is usually given as maintenance therapy for 6 months after post-remission therapy is
ATRA is usually given as maintenance therapy for 6 months after post-remission therapy is completed ATRA is usually given as maintenance therapy for 6 months after post-remission therapy is completed is incorrect. Recent evidence suggests that this no longer has a role following modern treatment for APML, although this is a little controversial.

ATRA should only be used during the acute period of DIC
ATRA should only be used during the acute period of DIC is incorrect. ATRA is used throughout the whole initial period of treatment until remission is achieved, ie normalisation of the bloodcount, with blasts and promyelocytes less than 5% in a post-induction bone marrow.

ATRA worsens the DIC picture
ATRA worsens the DIC picture is incorrect. ATRA will reduce DIC and therefore the risk of life-threatening bleeding.

stem: A 17-year-old girl undergoes a thrombophilia screen 1 week after discontinuing warfarin for a previous PE sustained while on the combined oral contraceptive pill. The results are as follows: protein C 40% (50–150), protein S 36% (50–150), antithrombin III 199 (50–150), APC resistance 1.4 (3–4). What further action will you take?
options: DNA analysis for Factor V Leiden
explanation:
Repeat thrombophilia screen 3 weeks later
This 16-year-old girl has only been off warfarin for a week before the thrombophilia screen was taken. Protein Cand protein S levels are low. However, protein C and protein S are vitamin K dependent, and therefore to obtain a meaningful result, the results should be repeated after a substantial amount of time when the patient is off warfarin.

DNA analysis for Factor V Leiden
DNA analysis for Factor V Leiden is incorrect. The whole area of thrombophilia screening is very controversial. One could argue that a thrombophilia screen is not really indicated in this situation at all. Current guidance suggests that results of a thrombophilia screen do not help in determining intensity or duration of anticoagulation.

Family study
Family study is incorrect. Family study is not required in the situation described and repeating the probably falsely low protein C and protein S levels would be the first management step.

Reintroduce anticoagulants
Reintroduce anticoagulants is incorrect. Reintroducing anticoagulants is a difficult issue. Recent publications do suggest that calculating a DASH score may help in this decision-making process, but patients who sustain a venous thrombotic event while on the oral contraceptive pill have a lower risk of recurrence if this medication is stopped. The decision to reintroduce anticoagulation needs to be made on a case-by-case basis.This will be determined by ongoing risk factors for further venous thrombotic events, balanced against any other risk factors for bleeding.The patient’s wishes and lifestyle factors will also need to be taken into consideration.

Screen for the prothrombin polymorphism
Screen for the prothrombin polymorphism is incorrect. This is a common mutation, which is present in about 2% of the UK population. Even if it was found, this would not usually influence the decision whether or not to reintroduce anticoagulants at this point in time.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to control her bleeding?
explanation:
Fresh frozen plasma
Fresh frozen plasma would be the next most appropriate step. This women is febrile and may well have sepsis from a urinary source. Her coagulation is very disordered, and couldwell be due to disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). In this situation, fresh frozen plasma is required, particularly in the presence of bleeding.

4 units of packed cells
4 units of packed cells is incorrect. Clearly this would be an appropriate step for someone with active bleeding, although of more urgency is correction of the disordered coagulation.

IV antibiotics
IV antibiotics is incorrect. IV antibiotics would be important, but in this situation, control of bleeding with frozen plasma would be the initial treatment of choice.

Platelet transfusion
Platelet transfusion is incorrect. The platelet count is 55 x 10 9/l, and platelets would only be given if the platelet count was less than 50 in the presence of active bleeding.

Prothrombin complex concentrate
Prothrombin complex concentrate is incorrect. Prothrombin complex concentrate is only given to patients on warfarin who have evidence of life-threatening bleeding. Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation You are asked to audit the use of low molecular weight versus unfractionated heparin in the hospital and provide commentary on the rationale for choosing between the two agents.

stem: A 17-year-old girl from Nigeria who recently immigrated to England has been referred by her GP because she looks anaemic. On examination you notice frontal bossing of the skull and chronic leg ulcers. Her Hb is 70 g/l (120–160 g/l) and Howell–Jolly bodies are seen. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Sickle-cell disease
We are told that the girl is anaemic with Howell–Jolly bodies seen on the peripheral blood film. Howell–Jolly bodies are a sign of hyposplenism, which is found in children and adolescents with sickle-cell anaemia. The sickle cells cause splenic infarction, which results in a hyposplenic state. Leg ulcers are also associated with sickle-cell disease.

Acute lymphocytic leukaemia
Acute lymphocytic leukaemia is incorrect. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is certainly possible in a 15-year-old patient, but again causes a pancytopenic state, or blasts in the peripheral blood. Again there are no particular associations with one ethnic group.

Aplastic anaemia
Aplastic anaemia is incorrect. Aplastic anaemia has no particular ethnic association. This is usually associated with a pancytopenic state, and acquired aplastic anaemia is rare in 15-year-old patients. This would not be associated with Howell–Jolly bodies in the peripheral blood.

Myeloma
Myeloma is incorrect. Myeloma is extremely rare in this age group. Again it would not cause a hyposplenic state.

Thalassaemia
Thalassaemia is incorrect. This usually does not result in a hyposplenic state, and therefore it would be unusual to see Howell–Jolly bodies in the peripheral blood. The spleen is enlarged because of haematopoiesis.

stem: Enoxaparin has just been recommended as the low molecular weight heparin of choice in your hospital trust. Which of the following represents the primary mechanism of action for low molecular weight heparin?
explanation:
Binds to anti-thrombin III
The primary mechanism of action for low molecular weight heparin is binding to anti-thrombin. Low molecular weight heparins inhibit the coagulation process through binding to anti-thrombin via a pentasaccharide sequence. This binding leads to a conformational change of anti-thrombin, which accelerates its inhibition of activated Xa.

Binds to factor II
Binds to factor II is incorrect. Binding to factor II, also known as prothrombin, is false. The primary mechanism of action for low molecular weight heparin is binding to anti-thrombin.

Binds to factor VIII
Binds to factor VIII is incorrect. The primary mechanism of action for low molecular weight heparin is binding to anti-thrombin.

Binds to factor X
Binds to factor X is incorrect. The primary mechanism of action for low molecular weight heparin is binding to anti-thrombin.Binds to Von Willebrand factor (VWF)
Binds to Von Willebrand factor (VWF) is incorrect. The primary mechanism of action for low molecular weight heparin is binding to anti-thrombin.

stem: A 28-year-old man with known von Willebrand's disease visits the dentist for a tooth extraction. Which of the following requires approval by a Heamatologist before instigating in this patient?
explanation:
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
The use of any NSAID must be discussed beforehand with the patient's Haematologist because of their effect on platelet aggregation. von Willebrand's disease arises from a deficiency in the quality or quantity of von Willebrand factor (vWF), a multimeric protein that is required for platelet adhesion.

Oxidised cellulose
Oxidised cellulose is a water-insoluble derivative of cellulose. It may contain carboxylic acid, aldehyde, and/or ketone groups, in addition to the original hydroxyl groups of cellulose, depending on the nature of the oxidant and reaction conditions. It is an anti-haemorrhagic agent and may, therefore, stop any bleeding seen with von Willebrand's disease.

Suturing
Suturing will provide a physical barrier to limit any bleeding from blood vessels damaged during a tooth extraction. A discussion about this with the patient's Haematologist is therefore not as frequently needed.

Anti-fibrinolytic agents
Antifibrinolytics are medicines that inhibit fibrinolysis (ie they inhibit the breakdown of clot formation). Examples include aminocaproic acid (ε-aminocaproic acid) and tranexamic acid. These lysine-like drugs interfere with the formation of the fibrinolytic enzyme, plasmin, from its precursor, plasminogen, by plasminogen activators. Their use may, therefore, stop any bleeding seen with von Willebrand's disease.

Lignocaine
There are no restrictions regarding the type of local anaesthetic agent used in dental surgery for patients with von Willebrand's disease; local anaesthetics mixed with vasoconstrictors (eg epinephrine) may provide additional local haemostasis.

stem: You suspect invasive aspergillosis. Which of the following is the most useful test to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
Galactomannan test
Galactomannan test is the most useful test to confirm the diagnosis of likely invasive aspergillosis. Galactomannan is a component of the aspergillus cell wall, and this can be detected in the bloodstream by an ELISA test.

Aspergillus IgE
Aspergillus IgE is incorrect. Aspergillus IgE is not the most useful test to confirm the likely diagnosis of aspergillosis; the galactomannan assay is much more useful.

Aspergillus IgG
Aspergillus IgG is incorrect. Aspergillus IgG is not the most useful test to confirm the likely diagnosis of aspergillosis; the galactomannan assay is much more useful.

Positive skin test for aspergillus
Positive skin test for aspergillus is incorrect. Skin testing for aspergillus does not confirm invasive aspergillosis.

Sputum eosinophils
Sputum eosinophils is incorrect. Sputum eosinophils will not confirm the diagnosis of invasive aspergillosis, and a positive galactomannan result is much more helpful in this situation.

stem: Blood film reveals a leukoerythroblastic picture with tear drop cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Myelofibrosis
Myelofibrosis is the correct answer. There are only two major causes of gross splenomegaly.These are chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) and myelofibrosis. To distinguish these two conditions, it is necessary to look at the white cell count. In CML, the white cell count is usually significantly raised, often greater than 100 ×10 9/l or even higher. In contrast, the white cell count in myelofibrosis can sometimes be slightly raised, but is more often normal or even reduced. In terms of the other blood film findings, a leucoerythroblastic blood picture with teardrop cells is entirely typical of the diagnosis of myelofibrosis.

Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia
Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is incorrect. This patient’s white cell count is normal and we are not told that he has a lymphocytosis in his peripheral blood. This does not usually give rise to gross splenomegaly.

Hodgkin’s lymphoma
Hodgkin’s lymphoma is incorrect. Hodgkin’s lymphoma usually gives rise to painless lymphadenopathy, usually above the diaphragm. Again, anaemia is rare, and gross splenomegaly is not seen.

Myelodysplasia
Myelodysplasia is incorrect. Myelodysplasia often results in anaemia with other cytopaenias. It does not give rise to gross splenomegaly.

Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma
Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma is incorrect. Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma again gives rise to lymphadenopathy, which is not described in this patient. It can give rise to splenomegaly, but rarely is it gross. The fact that the bloodfilm is leucoerythroblastic with teardrop cells suggests bone marrow infiltration, all of which are entirely typical of myelofibrosis.

stem: A patient with kidney failure presents with worsening anaemia. Which one of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Erythropoietin deficiency
Patients with kidney failure do not produce erythropoietin normally, and they often need erythropoietin supplementation to raise their haemoglobin levels.

Folate deficiency
Folate deficiency is incorrect. Folate deficiency is not particularly linked to kidney failure.

Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor deficiency
Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (GCSF) deficiency is incorrect. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor deficiency has got nothing to do with kidney failure. GCSF can be given by subcutaneous injection following intensive chemotherapy to stimulate neutrophil recovery, but this does not have anything to do with red cells.

Iron deficiency
Iron deficiency is incorrect. Iron deficiency can occur in kidney failure patients, and indeed patients need to be iron replete before starting erythropoietin supplements. However, erythropoietin deficiency is the major cause of anaemia in patients with kidney failure. Anaemia of Chronic Kidney DiseaseA 42-year-old gentleman with pyrexia of unknown origin is being investigated. He received a renal transplant 3.5 years previously, where the donor was CMV antibody positive, EBV antibody positive, HIV negative. On examination he has enlarged axillary lymph nodes. His bloods are as follows: Investigations Results Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) 100 g/l 135 - 175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 9.2 x 10 9/l 4 - 11 x 10 9/l Platelets (PLT) 135 x 10 9/l 150 - 400 x 10 9/l Creatinine 120 μmol/l (3 years ago was 110) 50 - 120 µmol/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 50 mm/h 0-10 mm in the 1 st hour Which one of the following is the likely cause?

Pyridoxine deficiency
Pyridoxine deficiency is incorrect. Pyridoxine deficiency is not specifically associated with kidney failure. Pyridoxine is one form of vitamin B6.

stem: She is febrile at 37.5°C with a widespread macular rash that extends from the palms and soles to involve the trunk and lower extremities. For the last 36 hours she has had profuse diarrhoea with some mixed blood. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Acute graft-versus-host disease
The onset of acute graft-versus-host disease is in the first 100 days post-transplant. Acute graft-versus-host disease typically causes a skin rash that in particular starts on the palms and soles. There is also associated diarrhoea and jaundice. This is a significant problem, and may result in widespread fluid loss from the bowel. It is more common after unrelated donor transplantation, than after a sibling allogeneic donor transplant. This is treated with immunosuppression, starting with high-dose steroids.

Acute graft rejection
Acute graft rejection is incorrect. Acute graft rejection would cause an ongoing pancytopenia, but the patient is only 24 days following the transplant, and there does appear to be neutrophil engraftment, with neutrophils of 0.8 × 10 9/l. The graft rejection would not be associated with the profuse diarrhoea that is typical of acute graftversus-host disease.

Cytomegalovirus infection
Cytomegalovirus infection is incorrect. Cytomegalovirus infection is usually an asymptomatic infection that is detected by rising PCR transcript levels in the post-transplant setting. The combination of the widespread macular rash and diarrhoea is much more compatible with acute graft-versus-host disease.

Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction
Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction is incorrect. A delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction would not result in the profuse diarrhoea and the widespread macular rash.

Thrombotic thrombocytopaenic purpura
Thrombotic thrombocytopaenic purpura is incorrect. Thrombotic thrombocytopaenia purpura can occur in the post-transplant setting. This can cause fevers, and will also result in neurological signs and renal impairment. This would not, however, lead to profuse diarrhoea and a rash.

stem: A 40-year-old patient has been complaining of headache, weakness, dizziness, pruritus and weight loss. His laboratory results show erythrocytosis, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis and a very low erythropoietin level. Apart from thrombosis, which one of the following is the major complication of this disease?
explanation:
Bleeding
This man has primary polycythaemia. Bleeding and thrombosis are the major complications of this condition. Peptic ulcer disease can occur and contributes to gastrointestinal bleeding. Thrombosis can either be venous or arterial in nature.

Fractures
Fractures is incorrect. Fractures are not a common feature or complication of this disease.

Hepatic failure
Hepatic failure is incorrect. Hepatic failure is not a feature of primary polycythaemia.

Kidney disease
Kidney disease is incorrect. Kidney disease is not a feature of primary polycythaemia. Polycythaemia Vera

Respiratory failure
Respiratory failure is incorrect. Respiratory failure is not a feature of primary polycythaemia.

stem: p a(O 2) 6.6 kPa p a(CO 2) 3.8 kPa Which underlying clotting disorder is most likely to be the cause of his presentation on this occasion?
explanation:
Protein S deficiency
Protein S deficiency has been described in the nephrotic syndrome. This is an acquired deficiency, due to loss of free protein S in the urine. This, along with the loss of anti-thrombin via the kidney, could contribute to the prothrombotic state.

Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome
Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome is incorrect. Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome is not associated with the risk of venous thrombosis in the nephrotic syndrome for similar reasons to factor V Leiden mutation.

Factor V Leiden mutation
Factor V Leiden mutation is incorrect. Factor V Leiden mutation is not associated with an increased venous thrombotic risk in the nephrotic syndrome. This risk occurs because of loss of the natural anticoagulants as part of the proteinuria seen in the nephrotic syndrome, rather than this mutation in the factor V gene.

Occult pelvic malignancy
Occult pelvic malignancy is incorrect. There is no suggestion of occult pelvic malignancy given in the question.

Protein C deficiency
Protein C deficiency is incorrect. Protein C deficiency is not well described in the nephrotic syndrome. Venous Thrombosis A 63-year-old man from Ghana presents with backache, lethargy and thirst. His erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is raised with normocytic normochromic anaemia.

stem: A 35-year-old man attends the Haematology Clinic having found a lump in his neck. He feels generally unwell but has no past history. There is axillary lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. Full blood count shows: WCC 16 × 10 3/mm 3; Hb 83 g/l; platelets 106 × 10 3/mm 3. The blood film and bone marrow aspirate show lymphoblasts. Which one of the following is the most useful test to make a definitive diagnosis?
explanation:
Immunophenotyping
Immunophenotyping is the correct answer because it provides detailed information about the specific types of cells present by identifying surface markers unique to different lymphoid or myeloid cells. It is essential for classifying the lymphoblasts as immature B-cells or T-cells, thereby confirming a diagnosis of ALL. Immunophenotyping can distinguish ALL from other haematologic malignancies like acute myeloid leukaemia or mature B-cell neoplasms. This test is crucial for guiding treatment decisions and prognostic considerations, making it the most definitive diagnostic tool in this case.

Cytogenetic analysis
Cytogenetic analysis is incorrect because while it plays a crucial role in risk stratification and prognosis determination in ALL, it does not make the initial definitive diagnosis. Cytogenetics can identify chromosomal abnormalities such as the Philadelphia chromosome, which can influence treatment decisions. However, it is secondary to identifying the nature of the lymphoblasts. It does not provide the necessary information to distinguish between different types of immature blood cells.

Lymph node biopsy
A lymph node biopsy is incorrect in this scenario because the presence of lymphoblasts in the bone marrow already indicates a systemic process, making the biopsy unnecessary for diagnosis. While lymph node biopsy can be useful in diagnosing lymphomas, it is not needed when marrow disease is evident. The biopsy would provide information about the lymph node tissue but not about the specific type of lymphoblasts present in the marrow. It is less informative compared to immunophenotyping for differentiating between types of leukaemia.

Total-body computed tomography (CT) scan
A CT scan is incorrect because it primarily shows anatomical details and the extent of lymphadenopathy, which is useful for staging rather than diagnosis. While it can provide a comprehensive view of the spread of disease, it does not identify the type of cells involved. CT scans are excellent for visualising structural abnormalities but cannot differentiate between different types of lymphoblasts or provide information on their immunologic markers. Thus, it does not contribute to establishing the definitive nature of the haematologic malignancy.

Total-body positron-emission tomography (PET) scan
A PET scan is incorrect because it measures metabolic activity and can identify areas of high cellular turnover, which might suggest malignancy but does not specify the type. PET scans are useful in staging and assessing the metabolic activity of known tumours or lymphadenopathy but do not provide cellular or molecular details required for diagnosis. The scan can show active disease regions but cannot determine if those regions are due to ALL, lymphoma or another condition. It lacks the specificity needed for diagnosing the type of lymphoblasts present.

stem: A 63-year-old man from Ghana presents with backache, lethargy and thirst. His erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is raised with normocytic normochromic anaemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Multiple myeloma
Myeloma should be considered in an elderly gentleman with back pain, thirst (probably due to hypercalcaemia), raised ESR (due to a paraprotein) and anaemia of chronic disease. Multiple myeloma is a malignant proliferation of plasma cells. It is more common in Afro-Caribbeans. Lytic lesions in the bones cause bone pain, fractures and hypercalcaemia. Patients may also have a raised ESR (with usually normal CRP) and kidney disease.

Calcium pyrophosphate arthropathy
Calcium pyrophosphate arthropathy is incorrect. Calcium pyrophosphate arthropathy or pseudogout particularly targets peripheral joints such as the knee or wrist. Raised ESR and anaemia are not features.

Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis is incorrect. Osteoarthritis is not associated with a raised ESR or anaemia.

Osteoporosis
Osteoporosis is incorrect. Osteoporosis is not common in elderly males, unless there is hypogonadism and it is not associated with a raised ESR or anaemia.

Paget’s disease of bone
Paget’s disease of bone is incorrect. Paget’s disease classically presents with bone pain, bone deformity, deafness and pathological fractures. The common biochemical abnormality is an isolated elevated raised alkaline phosphatase.

stem: A 38-year-old man presents with worsening tiredness, night sweats, cough and pruritus. His full blood count shows eosinophilia of 1800/μl (40–400 per μl). His GP checked his FBC 6 months ago, which reveals an eosinophil count of 1500/μl. He has no known allergies. There is no evidence of parasite detected in multiple stool samples. Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Corticosteroids
Corticosteroids here is probably the most correct answer. All we are told is that this man has eosinophilia. We are also told there is no evidence of parasite in his stool. Apart from that though, we do not have an actual diagnosis. This man actually needs a bone marrow examination to find out whether or not he has a clonal abnormality within his marrow. If there are no reactive causes for the eosinophilia, there are no clonal bone marrow problems either, then one could label him as having idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome. In this situation, the patient is best treated with immunosuppression in the form of steroids.

Ampicillin
Ampicillin is incorrect as there is no reason to suggest an infective aetiology in this question.

Cyclophosphamide
Cyclophosphamide is incorrect, because corticosteroids are the treatment of choice for idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome.

Interferon-alpha
Interferon-alpha is incorrect because this is not a treatment for hypereosinophilic syndrome.

Methotrexate
Methotrexate is incorrect because the initial choice of immunosuppression in the hypereosinophilic syndrome is corticosteroids.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a six-month history of recurrent episodes of passing black, tarry stools and occasional lightheadedness. He denies any weight loss or abdominal pain. His medical history includes hypertension and chronic kidney disease stage 3. Which is the best initial diagnostic test to confirm the most likely underlying cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Upper GI endoscopy
Upper GI endoscopy is the best initial diagnostic test for evaluating black, tarry stools (melena), which usually indicate an upper gastrointestinal source of bleeding. This procedure allows for direct visualization of the oesophagus, stomach, and duodenum and provides the opportunity for therapeutic intervention if needed, such as treating peptic ulcers, gastritis, or oesophagal varices. Given the patient's symptoms, an upper GI endoscopy is the most appropriate first step to confirm the underlying cause of his bleeding.

Abdominal CT scan
An abdominal CT scan may provide information about structural abnormalities or masses within the abdomen but is not sensitive enough to detect vascular lesions like angiodysplasia. While it might reveal other potential causes of recurrent GI bleeding such as diverticulitis, it does not offer direct visualisation nor therapeutic options for angiodysplastic lesions.

Capsule endoscopy
Capsule endoscopy can be useful in detecting small bowel sources of obscure GI bleeding. However, it is typically reserved for cases where both upper and lower GI endoscopies have failed to identify a source. It has limited utility as an initial investigation, given its inability to intervene therapeutically during diagnosis.

Colonoscopy
While a colonoscopy is valuable for evaluating sources of lower GI bleeding such as diverticulosis, colorectal cancer, or inflammatory bowel disease, it is not the best initial test in this scenario. The patient's presentation with black, tarry stools (melena) typically indicates bleeding from an upper gastrointestinal source. Therefore, an upper GI endoscopy is more appropriate as the initial diagnostic approach to identify and potentially treat the source of bleeding.

Mesenteric angiography
Mesenteric angiography could be considered if there is active significant bleeding that cannot be localised by less invasive methods like colonoscopy or upper GI endoscopy. However, it involves higher risk due to its invasive nature and radiation exposure and, therefore, is not suitable as an initial diagnostic approach without prior evaluation using safer modalities.

stem: A 22-year-old woman from the USA falls profoundly ill while visiting relatives in the UK. She is admitted unconscious with a purpuric rash after waking earlier complaining of severe headache and neck pain. She currently takes 20 mg prednisolone. On examination she has abdominal laparoscopic scars and her blood film shows hyposplenic features. What is the most likely indication for this woman’s prior splenectomy?
explanation:
Immune thrombocytopaenic purpura
This is quite a difficult question. We are told that this lady has a purpuric rash, headache and neck pain. This would be consistent with the development of meningitis, with meningococcal sepsis. We are told that this lady has a prior splenectomy, and the blood film shows hyposplenic features. This has been done through a laparoscopic approach in the past. Immune thrombocytopaenic purpura is the most likely indication for this woman’s prior splenectomy. It is a very effective operation for immune thrombocytopaenia that has not responded to first-line steroids.

Beta-thalassaemia trait
Beta-thalassaemia trait is incorrect. Beta-thalassaemia trait is an asymptomatic condition, leading to a mild hypochromic microcytic anaemia, and splenectomy is not indicated for this.

Gaucher’s disease
Gaucher’s disease is incorrect. Gaucher’s disease does cause splenomegaly, but treatment is with replacement enzyme therapy, and would not be a very common reason to perform a splenectomy.

Hodgkin’s disease
Hodgkin’s disease is incorrect. Open splenectomy and lymph node biopsies were performed up until the mid1970s. This was to document the stage of the disease before the invention of CT scans.

Sickle cell disease
Sickle cell disease is incorrect. Sickle cell disease results in an asplenic state due to progressive splenic infarction because of the repeated vaso-occlusive events in the splenic micro-circulation. Splenectomy is therefore not indicated in sickle cell disease.

stem: A 49-year-old man returns from working abroad with a recent diagnosis of chronic myeloid leukaemia. You are considering a trial of the drug imatinib. Which one of the following statements best fits the advice and information to be given regarding the use of imatinib?
options: Gynaecomastia never occurs in patients taking imatinib
It is recommended by NICE for Philadelphia chromosome-negative patients
Nausea is common in patients taking imatinib
NICE recommends not initiating therapy in the accelerated phase
explanation:
Nausea is common in patients taking imatinib
Nausea is common in patients with imatinib, but is usually easily managed.

Constipation is a common side-effect
Constipation is a common side effect is incorrect. Diarrhoea is more common.

Gynaecomastia never occurs in patients taking imatinib
Gynaecomastia never occurs in patients taking imatinib is incorrect. Gynaecomastia has been reported in patients taking imatinib.

It is recommended by NICE for Philadelphia chromosome-negative patients
It is recommended by NICE for Philadelphia chromosome-negative patients is incorrect. Imatinib targets the abnormal tyrosine kinase.

NICE recommends not initiating therapy in the accelerated phase
NICE recommends not initiating therapy in the accelerated phase is incorrect. The NICE recommendations are that it can be used in the accelerated phase of the disease.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?
explanation:
Piperacillin and tazobactam
NICE defines neutropaenic sepsis as a temperature of higher than 38 °C or other signs or symptoms consistent with clinically significant sepsis, in association with a neutrophil count of 0.5 × 10 9 or lower in a patient having anti-cancer treatment. NICE guidelines are very clear with respect to initial therapy of neutropaenic sepsis: ‘Offer beta lactam monotherapy with piperacillin with tazobactam as initial empiric antibiotic therapy to patients with suspected neutropenic sepsis who need intravenous treatment unless there are patient-specific or local microbiological contraindications. ‘Do not offer an aminoglycoside, either as monotherapy or in dual therapy, for the initial empiric treatment of suspected neutropenic sepsis unless there are patient-specific or local microbiological indications.’ Only this option contains piperacillin and tazobactam, so this is the only appropriate option. The guidelines also recommend that within 24 h of presentation to secondary or tertiary care, patients should be managed by an oncology specialist (ie handed over to the specialist oncology firm at the latest the day after admission).

Cefuroxime and gentamicin
Cefuroxime and gentamicin is incorrect. Cefuroxime and gentamicin does not contain piperacillin and tazobactam so is not appropriate unless there are patient-specific or local microbiological indications.

Ciprofloxacin and vancomycin
Ciprofloxacin and vancomycin is incorrect. Ciprofloxacin and vancomycin does not contain piperacillin and tazobactam so is not appropriate unless there are patient-specific or local microbiological indications.

Gentamicin and teicoplanin
Gentamicin and teicoplanin is incorrect. Gentamicin and teicoplanin does not contain piperacillin and tazobactam so is not appropriate unless there are patient-specific or local microbiological indications.

Vancomycin and gentamicin
Vancomycin and gentamicin is incorrect. Vancomycin and gentamicin does not contain piperacillin and tazobactam so is not appropriate unless there are patient-specific or local microbiological indications.

stem: A 48-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review. She has not had a period for some 5 months and has been suffering from depressed mood, decreased sex drive and sweats at night. She has read about the benefits of HRT when used in the peri-menopausal period and wants to discuss options for HRT with you. Which of the following fits best with the risks of HRT?
options: The risk of colorectal cancer is doubled
The risk of ovarian cancer is doubled
There is at least a doubling of risk of DVT.
There is at least a doubling of the risk of stroke
There is one extra case of breast cancer per 100 women per annum who take HRT
explanation:
There is at least a doubling of risk of DVT.
Patients taking HRT are at 2–3 times the risk of DVT compared to similar individuals not taking HRT.

The risk of colorectal cancer is doubled
The risk of colorectal cancer is incorrect. The risk of colorectal cancer may be reduced in patients taking HRT.

The risk of ovarian cancer is doubled
With regards to ovarian cancer is incorrect. With regards to ovarian cancer there is conflicting evidence with respect to either a small increase or no harm with HRT prescription.

There is at least a doubling of the risk of stroke
The risk of stroke is incorrect. The risk of stroke appears to be increased in women above the age of 60 who are taking HRT. For women under 60 there does not appear to be an increased risk of stroke.

There is one extra case of breast cancer per 100 women per annum who take HRT
With regards to breast cancer is incorrect. With regards to breast cancer there is one extra case per 1000 women per annum who take HRT. Venous Thrombosis A 32-year-old woman who has undergone multiple previous blood transfusions develops transfusion related acute lung injury, (TRALI), shortly after beginning a blood transfusion.

stem: Which haemopoietic growth factor is most likely to lead to improvement in her neutrophil count?
explanation:
G-CSF
G-CSF is the growth factor that is most likely to lead to an improvement in her neutrophil count. This stands for granulocyte-colony stimulating factor. This is routinely given after intensive chemotherapy for acute leukaemia and following stem-cell transplants. It can be given in other situations, such as auto-immune neutropenia, when it is necessary to raise the neutrophil count and there is associated sepsis.

Erythropoietin
Erythropoietin is incorrect. This stimulates red blood cell production.

IL-3
IL-3 is incorrect. This stimulates the differentiation of multi-potent haemopoetic stem cells into myeloid progenitor cells. It is also not routinely available, unlike G-CSF which is routinely available in the clinical situation.

SCF (stem-cell factor)
Stem-cell factor is incorrect. As the term suggests, it plays an important role in the regulation of haemopoetic stem cells in the bone marrow.

Thrombopoietin
Thrombopoietin is incorrect. This stimulates platelet production.

stem: Bone marrow examination is suggestive of chronic myeloid leukaemia and Ph chromosome positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
explanation:
Imatinib
Imatinib is indicated as first-line treatment for chronic myeloid leukaemia. One-third of patients, however, do not achieve an optimal outcome and require alternative therapies due to the emergence of drug resistance.

Allogenic stem cell transplant
Before the introduction of tyrosine kinase inhibitors, allogeneic stem cell transplantation was the initial treatment of chronic myeloid leukaemia for those patients who were fit enough to tolerate this procedure. It would not be appropriate initial therapy.

Dasatinib
Second-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitors (eg dasatinib) are recommended in chronic myeloid leukaemia if there is treatment failure with imatinib, as evidenced by first-line tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) response milestones, considering BCR-ABL1 amounts. Dasatinib has 325-fold higher potency in vivo, with inhibitory activity against the majority of imatinib-resistant BCR-ABL mutants.

Nilotinib
Nilotinib was designed to have enhanced selectivity and potency towards BCR-ABL, with clinical activity against the majority of resistant mutations to imatinib. It was recommended as second-line therapy for patients resistant to, or intolerant of, imatinib therapy.

Ponatinib
Ponatinib, although a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), is generally reserved for patients who have either failed treatment with, or become intolerant of, other TKIs or who carry the T315KD mutation. Chronic Myeloid Leukaemia A 42-year-old lady, with known von Willebrand disease, is awaiting a dental extraction. A previous tooth extraction was complicated by profuse bleeding, and required a two-unit blood transfusion. Apart from menorrhagia and easy bruising when she has been involved in contact sports, she has had no other particular problems.

stem: Which of the following is the next most appropriate investigation to confirm the cause of this lymphocytosis?
explanation:
Peripheral blood flow cytometry immunophenotyping
Peripheral blood flow cytometry, also known as immunophenotyping, is the next most appropriate investigation to confirm the cause of his lymphocytosis. Immunophenotyping looks at the expression of proteins on the surface of the lymphocytes. The most likely diagnosis here is early-stage chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL). The lymphocytes in CLL express certain proteins on the surface, which can be characterised by immunophenotyping. The advantage is that this can be done on peripheral blood, which is not invasive, with results readily available in a few hours or days.

Bone marrow aspiration
Bone marrow aspiration is incorrect. Bone marrow aspiration is an invasive procedure and this is not required. Investigating cell surface markers in the peripheral blood is much less invasive and certainly is the first-line investigation to confirm the cause of the lymphocytosis. If cell surface markers suggested perhaps an underlying lymphoma, then at that point in time a bone marrow examination may be required, but it is not the first investigation in this patient.

CT abdomen
CT abdomen is incorrect. CT scan of the abdomen is not a first-line investigation. Although this may show lymphadenopathy, this will not help to distinguish between CLL and other lymphoproliferative disorders.

LDH
LDH is incorrect. LDH elevation is a non-specific finding for haematological malignancies. It is usually normal in CLL, and this investigation again does not distinguish CLL from other lymphoproliferative disorders.

Lymph node biopsy
Lymph node biopsy is incorrect. Lymph node biopsy is an invasive procedure, and a lymph node biopsy is only required if there is evidence of rapidly progressive lymphadenopathy, or other features suggestive of a highgrade lymphoma.

stem: A 42-year-old lady, with known von Willebrand disease, is awaiting a dental extraction. A previous tooth extraction was complicated by profuse bleeding, and required a two-unit blood transfusion. Apart from menorrhagia and easy bruising when she has been involved in contact sports, she has had no other particular problems. What is the most appropriate prophylactic measure to use prior to the planned dental procedure?
explanation:
DDAVP
DDAVP enhances the release of pre-formed Von Willebrand factor and factor VIII, and is appropriate for such procedures such as a dental extraction. It is often combinedwith tranexamic acid.

Cryoprecipitate
Cryoprecipitate is incorrect. Cryoprecipitate is used to replace fibrinogen in patients with DIC.

FFP
FFP is incorrect. FFP is no longer used to treat Von Willebrand’s disease, due to the risks of viral contamination.

Human cleansed factor VIII
Human cleansed factor VIII is incorrect. Where possible blood products derived from donors should be avoided.

Recombinant factor VIII
Recombinant factor VIII is incorrect. Recombinant factor VIII would not give any Von Willebrand factor replacement. Often, concentrates that combine both factor VIII and Von Willebrand factor are required formore invasive procedures. DDAVP, along with tranexamic acid, is usually more appropriate for this more minor procedure.

stem: Which one of the following genetic abnormalities is associated with the worst prognosis?
explanation:
Chromosome 7 abnormalities
Chromosome 7 abnormalities are associated with the worst prognosis in this question. They are associated with a lower rate of complete remission, with a higher rate of relapsein acute myeloid leukaemia.

inv 16
inv 16 is incorrect. Inversion 16 is a sub-type of core binding factor leukaemia that is associated with a good prognosis.

t(8;21)
t(8;21) t(8:21) is incorrect. t(8:21) is another form of core binding factor leukaemia, again associated with a good overallprognosis in acute myeloid leukaemia.

t(15;17)
t(15;17) t(15:17) is incorrect. t(15:17) is the typical translocation found in acute promyelocytic leukaemia. This is associated with an excellent overall prognosis.

t(16;16)
t(16;16) t(16:16) is incorrect. t(16:16) is a form of core binding factor leukaemia associated with chromosome 16 abnormalities. This again is associated with a good overall prognosis. Acute Myeloid Leukaemia A 26-year-old woman with a history of factor V Leiden mutation presents to the Emergency Department with left sided pleuritic chest pain, O 2 saturation of 91%, BP of 90/60 mmHg, and tachycardia at 100 bpm. The medical personnel elect to thrombolyse her but the alteplase is given as a single rapid IV bolus rather than as a 2hr infusion. Within a few minutes she begins to bleed profusely from her rectum and has a larger upper GI haemorrhage. Her BP falls to 75/50 mmHg.

stem: A 26-year-old woman with a history of factor V Leiden mutation presents to the Emergency Department with left sided pleuritic chest pain, O 2 saturation of 91%, BP of 90/60 mmHg, and tachycardia at 100 bpm. The medical personnel elect to thrombolyse her but the alteplase is given as a single rapid IV bolus rather than as a 2hr infusion. Within a few minutes she begins to bleed profusely from her rectum and has a larger upper GI haemorrhage. Her BP falls to 75/50 mmHg. Which of the following is likely to be most effective in reversing the systemic effects of Alteplase?
explanation:
Tranexamic acid
The correct answer is Tranexamic acid. Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic compound, which is a potent competitive inhibitor of the activation of plasminogen to plasmin. At much higher concentrations it is a non-competitive inhibitor of plasmin. For these reasons it is the most appropriate initial option here.

FFP
FFP is incorrect. Although replacement may be required it is not a specific antifibrinolytic.

Protamine sulphate
Protamine sulphate is incorrect. Protamine sulphate is a drug for heparin reversal.

Prothrombin complex concentrate
Prothrombin complex concentrate is incorrect. Prothrombin complex concentrate is used for acute reversal of the effects of warfarin.

Vitamin K
Vitamin K is incorrect. Vitamin K is used for reversal of warfarin.

stem: A 42-year-old man from West Africa has recently begun dapsone therapy. He presents to the Emergency Department with anxiety, confusion, headache and shortness of breath at rest. He has no other past medical history of note. His BP is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 90 bpm and regular. He has pale sclera. Saturation is measured at 89% on pulse oximetry. You suspect he has methaemoglobinaemia. Which one of the following is the most likely cause?
options: Binding of Fe2+ to a sulfonate complex
explanation:
Oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+
This is what occurs in methaemoglobinaemia. The iron in haemoglobin is normally the ferrous Fe 2+ form. In methaemoglobinaemia, this is oxidised to the inactive ferric Fe 3+ form. Dapsone can act as an oxidising agent. There is a high prevalence of glucose-6 dehydrogenase deficiency in patients from West Africa.This may therefore result in increased oxidisation of the iron-containing component of haemoglobin, from Fe 2+ to Fe 3+.

Binding of Fe2+ to a sulfonate complex
Binding of Fe 2+ to a sulfonate complex is incorrect. Oxidation of Fe 2+ to Fe 3+ is what occurs in methaemoglobinaemia.

Oxidation of Fe+ to Fe2+
Oxidation of Fe + to Fe 2+ is incorrect. Oxidation of Fe 2+ to Fe 3+ is what occurs in methaemoglobinaemia.

Reduction of Fe2+ to Fe+
Reduction of Fe

Reduction of Fe3+ to Fe2+

stem: A 16-year-old young man with sickle cell anaemia is admitted with recent breathlessness. He is febrile and has a clear chest with saturations of 98% on air. From his outpatient notes his usual Hb is 90 g/l. FBC taken in the Emergency Department shows WCC 8.6 × 10 3/mm 3, Hb 47 g/l, platelets 573 × 10 3/mm 3 with a bilirubin 25 mmol/l. Which investigation is the most useful to perform next to identify the most likely underlying cause of this drop in haemoglobin levels?
explanation:
Reticulocyte count
A reticulocyte count will be the next most useful investigation. This is a very quick investigation to have performed, and is usually done at the same time as the full blood count, although it is not routinely reported. Essentially this young man has had a significant decline in his haemoglobin. This could be due to a significant episode of haemolytic anaemia, but equally well, could be due to an aplastic crisis, when the bone marrow stops producing red blood cells. A reticulocyte count would be very helpful to distinguish the two. When there is haemolysis occurring, one would imagine that the bone marrow would function appropriately, to try to produce increased amounts of red blood cells, therefore resulting in an increased reticulocyte count. In an aplastic crisis, the bone marrow will not be making red blood cells, resulting in a very low reticulocyte count.

Chest X-ray
Chest X-ray is incorrect. Chest X-ray will not distinguish between a haemolytic or an aplastic crisis.

Parvovirus serology
Parvovirus serology is incorrect. Parvovirus serology will take a number of days to come back, and will not be the first investigation in pointing to a possible aplastic crisis. While it is the most common it is not the only virus that can cause aplastic crisis.

Serum haptoglobin
Serum haptoglobin is incorrect. Serum haptoglobin often takes many days to turn around, and is usually only reduced in cases of intravascular haemolytic anaemia.

Urinary haemosiderin.

stem: Which one of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma
This man has evidence of lymphadenopathyin the supraclavicular region. He also has night sweats and acrocyanosis. His white cell count is slightly elevated, he is anaemic, and also has cold agglutinins present. Cold agglutinins are immunoglobulins that bind to red blood cells at cold temperatures, and can be associated with underlying lymphoproliferative disease. He therefore should have his lymph node biopsied to make the definitive diagnosis.

Bronchial carcinoma
Bronchial carcinoma is incorrect. Bronchial carcinoma is not typically associated with cold agglutinin disease. There is nothing else in the question to suggest this, such as a prolonged smoking history.

Drug-induced haemolysis
Drug-induced haemolysis is incorrect. Cold agglutinins are typically associated with an underlying lymphoproliferative disorder, and drug-induced haemolysis would not explain his lymphadenopathy.

Hodgkin’s disease
Hodgkin’s disease is incorrect. Hodgkin’s disease is relatively rare in this age group, and it is not associated with cold agglutinins or acrocyanosis.

Mycoplasma pneumonia
Mycoplasma pneumonia is incorrect. Mycoplasma pneumonia would not explain the significant fatigue, night sweats or left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma A 22-year-old woman from the USA falls profoundly ill while visiting relatives in the UK. She is admitted unconscious with a purpuric rash after waking earlier complaining of severe headache and neck pain. She currently takes 20 mg prednisolone. On examination she has abdominal laparoscopic scars and her blood film shows hyposplenic features.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?
explanation:
IV antibiotics
This lady has neutropaenic sepsis and needs urgent broad-spectrum antibiotics. This is a medical emergency and should be given within an hour of presentation.

Close observation
Close observation is incorrect. Close observation is insufficient intervention here. This is a medical emergency that requires broad-spectrum antibiotics.

G-CSF
G-CSF is incorrect. G-CSF may be required to reduce the period of neutropaenia, but the most pressing intervention is broad-spectrum antibiotics.

Packed red cells
Packed red cells is incorrect. Packed red cells is much less important that IV antibiotics, and the haemoglobin is only 85 g/l in a young woman. This would generally indicate that transfusion was not required at this haemoglobin level.

Platelets
Platelets is incorrect. Platelet transfusion is usually only given when platelets are less than 20 in the setting of fever, or less than 10 in the absence of fever. Therefore, this could be considered, but not as a first-line intervention before rapidly giving IV antibiotics.

stem: A 65-year-old patient has noticed worsening tiredness, weight loss and shortness of breath over the last 6 months. Lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly are present. His peripheral lymphocyte count is 60 × 10 9/l ((1.0– 3.0) × 10 9/l). Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step in obtaining the diagnosis?
explanation:
Blood smear examination with immunophenotyping
It is necessary to characterise the nature of the lymphocytes. This is done using a process called immunophenotyping, which looks at the different patterns of markers of proteins on the surface of the lymphocytes. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) has a very particular profile of antigens on the surface of the lymphocytes (typically expressing CD5, CD19, dim CD20, dim CD22, CD23, bright CD43, dim CD45, dim-tonegative CD79b, dim CD81, CD200 and dim monoclonal surface immunoglobulin), which allows the diagnosis to be made without the need for a bone marrow examination. This would, therefore, certainly be the first step in attaining the diagnosis. The word ‘appropriate’ is very important here. This is because it is the least invasive way of trying to understand the nature of the lymphocytosis.

Abdominal ultrasound
Abdominal ultrasound is incorrect. Although this might delineate further the extent of the lymphadenopathy, it would not help in obtaining a diagnosis.

Bone marrow biopsy
Bone marrow biopsy is incorrect. Bone marrow biopsy is not the most appropriate next step in obtaining the diagnosis because it is more invasive than taking a simple blood sample for immunophenotyping. Note that immunophenotyping is also termed ‘flow cytometry’.

CT abdomen
CT abdomen is incorrect. Although this might delineate the extent of the lymphadenopathy further, it would not help in obtaining a diagnosis.

Lymph node biopsy.

stem: A 27-year-old female is to receive 3 units of blood over 30 min to treat substantial blood loss after delivery. Shortly after the first unit commences she develops urticaria, shortness of breath and back pain. On examination her pulse is 160 bpm. Which one of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation:
ABO incompatibility
ABO incompatibility is the most likely cause of the patient’s current condition. The fact that this young lady has a significant tachycardia and back pain is entirely typical of an acute haemolytic transfusion reaction. ABO incompatibility has to be assumed until proved otherwise, with the transfusion being stopped immediately. The blood transfusion should be returned to the laboratory for further serological investigations, and the patient should be supported medically. Treatment may include the involvement of critical care, the renal team and potentially haemodialysis.

Anti-human leukocyte antigen antibodies
Anti-human leukocyte antigen (HLA) antibodies is incorrect. Once again, ABO incompatibility must be excluded as a matter of urgency given the clinical scenario.

Anti-neutrophil antibodies
Anti-neutrophil antibodies is incorrect. Anti-neutrophil antibodies cause febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reactions, which are usually characterised by fever and itching alone. This is not the case in this question.

Contamination
Contamination is incorrect. Contamination for example by bacteria, is false. The most urgent diagnosis to make is that of an ABO incompatible blood transfusion. It should be noted that platelet transfusions carry a higher risk of bacterial contamination than red blood cells. Platelets only have a limited life span of 5 days and need to be stored at room temperature, which promotes bacterial growth.
